items.q: Apa output kode berikut dan mengapa? (Stale Closure)

a.text: Output: Selalu print 0 meskipun button diklik berkali-kali.
Alasan: Ini adalah stale closure. useEffect dengan \[\] hanya dibuat sekali saat mount, sehingga count di dalam closure selalu mereferensikan nilai awal 0.
Solusi: gunakan useRef untuk menyimpan nilai terbaru

a.code:
const countRef = useRef(count);
useEffect(() => { countRef.current = count; }, [count]);

items.q: Apa perbedaan useLayoutEffect vs useEffect?

items: useEffect: dijalankan asynchronous setelah browser paint (tidak memblok rendering)
useLayoutEffect: dijalankan synchronous setelah DOM mutation tapi SEBELUM browser paint

a.text: Gunakan useLayoutEffect ketika perlu membaca layout DOM dan memicu re-render synchronously (misal: mengukur ukuran elemen, menghindari flickering).

modules.title: Kafka: Arsitektur, Topic, Partition & Offset
modules.summary: Apa itu Kafka, komponen inti, beda dengan message queue biasa, topic & partisi, offset, dan memilih jumlah partisi.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: What is Apache Kafka? Why is it used? ⭐

a.text: Apache Kafka is an open-source, distributed event streaming platform originally developed by LinkedIn and later donated to the Apache Software Foundation. It is designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant, real-time data streaming.
Key reasons Kafka is used:

items: **Event Streaming:** Real-time ingestion and processing of millions of events per second
**Decoupling:** Producers and consumers are independent; producers don't know about consumers
**Durability:** Messages are persisted to disk and replicated across brokers
**Scalability:** Horizontally scalable via partitioning across multiple brokers
**Fault Tolerance:** Replication ensures data availability even when brokers fail
**Replay:** Consumers can re-read past messages by resetting offsets

a.text: **Note:** *Kafka is not a traditional message queue — it is a distributed commit log optimized for sequential disk I/O.*

items.q: What are the core components of Kafka? ⭐

items: **Broker:** A Kafka server that stores messages. A Kafka cluster consists of multiple brokers
**Topic:** A named, ordered, immutable stream of records. Topics are split into partitions
**Partition:** An ordered, immutable sequence of records. Enables parallelism and scalability
**Producer:** A client that publishes (writes) records to a Kafka topic
**Consumer:** A client that subscribes to topics and reads records from partitions
**Consumer Group:** A group of consumers that jointly consume a topic; each partition is assigned to one consumer
**ZooKeeper / KRaft:** Manages cluster metadata, broker leadership, and configuration (ZooKeeper is legacy; KRaft is the modern replacement)
**Offset:** A sequential number identifying each record within a partition

items.q: What is the difference between Kafka and traditional message queues (e.g., RabbitMQ)?
What is a Kafka Topic? How does partitioning work? ⭐

a.text: A Topic is a category or feed name to which records are published. Topics in Kafka are:

items: Multi-subscriber: multiple consumers can read from the same topic
Durable: records are retained based on retention policy (time or size)
Partitioned: each topic is divided into one or more partitions for parallelism

a.text: Partitioning mechanics:

items: **Ordering:** Order is guaranteed only within a single partition, not across partitions
**Key-based routing:** Records with the same key always go to the same partition (murmur2 hash by default)
**Round-robin:** If no key, records are distributed across partitions round-robin
**Custom partitioner:** You can implement a custom Partitioner interface

items.q: What is an Offset in Kafka? How is it managed? ⭐

a.text: An offset is a unique, sequential integer assigned to each record within a partition. Offsets are:

items: Immutable: once assigned, an offset never changes
Per-partition: offset sequences are independent for each partition
Consumer-tracked: consumers store their current offset to know what to read next

a.text: Offset storage options:

items: **Auto-commit:** Kafka auto-commits offsets every auto.commit.interval.ms (default 5000ms)
**Manual commit:** Use commitSync() or commitAsync() for fine-grained control
**External store:** Store offsets in a database for exactly-once semantics

items.q: How do you choose the right number of partitions for a topic?

a.text: Choosing partition count involves trade-offs:

items: **Parallelism:** More partitions = more consumer threads can read in parallel
**Throughput:** Each partition is handled by one consumer in a group; more partitions = higher throughput
**Overhead:** Each partition has memory/file handle overhead on brokers and ZooKeeper
**Rule of thumb:** Start with max(target throughput / single partition throughput, consumer parallelism)
**Ordering requirements:** More partitions mean less strict ordering across the topic

a.text: **Note:** *You can increase partition count after creation, but you cannot decrease it. Increasing partitions changes the key-to-partition mapping, which can break ordering guarantees for keyed messages.*

modules.title: Kafka: Producer, Consumer & Consumer Group
modules.summary: Cara kerja producer, setting acks, idempotent producer & exactly-once, consumer group, rebalancing, auto.offset.reset, commitSync vs commitAsync.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: How does the Kafka Producer work internally? ⭐

a.text: The Kafka Producer follows a batching, async send pipeline:

items: **Serialization:** Key and value are serialized using configured serializers
**Partitioner:** Determines which partition to route the record to
**RecordAccumulator:** Records are batched into a buffer grouped by topic-partition (batch.size, linger.ms)
**Sender thread:** A background thread drains batches and sends them to brokers
**Acknowledgment:** Broker sends ack based on acks config; retries happen on failure

items.q: What are the acks settings in Kafka Producer? What are the trade-offs? ⭐

head: **acks Value**
**Behavior**
**Durability**
**Performance**
rows: Fire and forget — no ack waited
Moderate (loss if leader dies before replica sync)
Waits for all in-sync replicas (ISR) to ack

a.text: **Note:** *Use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 for production systems requiring no data loss.*

items.q: What is idempotent producer? How do you enable exactly- once semantics? ⭐

a.text: An idempotent producer ensures that retries do not result in duplicate messages. Each message gets a unique sequence number and producer ID (PID). If a retried batch has the same sequence number, the broker deduplicates it.

a.code:
props.put("enable.idempotence", "true");
// Also automatically sets: acks=all, retries=MAX_INT, max.in.flight=5

a.text: Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS) — full pipeline:

items: **Idempotent producer:** Deduplicates retries within a session
**Transactional producer:** Atomic writes across multiple partitions/topics
**Isolation level:** Consumer reads only committed transactions (read_committed)

items.q: How does the Kafka Consumer work? What is a Consumer Group? ⭐

a.text: Kafka Consumers use a pull model — they periodically poll the broker for new messages. The consumer maintains its position (offset) in each partition.
Consumer Group concepts:

items: Each consumer group has a unique group.id
Within a group, each partition is assigned to exactly ONE consumer
If consumers > partitions, some consumers will be idle
If consumers < partitions, some consumers will read from multiple partitions
Multiple groups can independently read the same topic (broadcast/fan-out pattern)

items.q: What is Consumer Rebalancing? What triggers it? ⭐

a.text: Rebalancing is the process of redistributing partition assignments among consumers in a group. It ensures all active consumers have a fair share of partitions.
Triggers for rebalancing:

items: A new consumer joins the group
A consumer leaves (explicitly or due to crash / heartbeat timeout)
A subscribed topic gets new partitions added
Consumer calls unsubscribe()

a.text: Impact of rebalancing:

items: During rebalance, ALL consumers in the group stop consuming (stop-the-world)
May cause duplicate processing if offsets weren't committed before the rebalance

a.text: Minimizing rebalance impact:

items: **session.timeout.ms:** Increase to avoid false timeouts (default: 45000ms)
**heartbeat.interval.ms:** Should be ~1/3 of session.timeout.ms
**max.poll.interval.ms:** Increase if processing is slow (default: 300000ms)
**Static membership:** Use group.instance.id to allow consumers to rejoin without triggering full rebalance

a.text: **Note:** *Kafka 2.4+ introduced incremental cooperative rebalancing (CooperativeStickyAssignor) which only revokes partitions that need to move, avoiding stop-the-world rebalances.*

items.q: What is the difference between auto.offset.reset=earliest vs latest?

items: **earliest:** Consumer starts reading from the beginning of the partition (offset 0 or lowest available). Used when you want to process all historical data.
**latest (default):** Consumer starts reading from the next new message produced after subscription. Historical messages are skipped.
**none:** Throws NoOffsetForPartitionException if no committed offset is found for the consumer group.

a.text: **Note:** *This setting only applies when a consumer group has NO committed offsets. If a committed offset exists, reading resumes from that offset regardless of auto.offset.reset.*

items.q: What is the difference between commitSync() and commitAsync()?

head: **Method**
**Behavior**
**Performance**
**Error Handling**
rows: Blocks until broker confirms commit; retries on failure
Automatic retry; throws exception on final failure
Non-blocking; fires and forgets commit to broker
No automatic retry; use callback for error logging
Use commitAsync() in loop; commitSync() on shutdown

modules.title: Kafka: Replikasi, Keandalan & Tuning
modules.summary: Replikasi & ISR, min.insync.replicas, saat broker mati, konfigurasi producer/consumer untuk throughput tinggi, dan rahasia kecepatan Kafka.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: How does Kafka replication work? ⭐

a.text: Kafka replicates each partition across multiple brokers for fault tolerance:

items: **Leader:** Each partition has one leader that handles all reads and writes
**Followers:** Follower replicas passively copy data from the leader
**ISR (In-Sync Replicas):** The set of replicas that are fully caught up with the leader
**Replication Factor:** Number of total replicas (including leader). Recommended: 3 in production

a.text: Leader election:

items: If a leader fails, Kafka elects a new leader from the ISR
If ISR is empty and unclean.leader.election.enable=true, an out-of-sync replica can become leader (data loss risk)
unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default since Kafka 0.11) prevents data loss at the cost of availability

items.q: What is min.insync.replicas and why is it important? ⭐

a.text: min.insync.replicas (minISR) is a broker/topic configuration specifying the minimum number of in-sync replicas that must acknowledge a write for it to be considered successful (only enforced when acks=all).
Example scenario with RF=3:

items: min.insync.replicas=2 means at least 2 replicas (leader + 1 follower) must be in-sync
If only 1 replica is in-sync, the producer gets NotEnoughReplicasException
This prevents data loss even if a broker fails immediately after write

a.text: **Note:** *Golden rule for production: replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all. This tolerates 1 broker failure with zero data loss.*

items.q: What happens when a Kafka broker goes down?

a.text: When a broker fails:

items: ZooKeeper (or KRaft controller) detects the failure via missed heartbeats
For each partition where the failed broker was the LEADER, a new leader is elected from ISR
Producers and consumers automatically reconnect and redirect to new partition leaders
For partitions where the failed broker was a FOLLOWER, no leader election is needed; ISR shrinks
When the broker recovers, it re-joins as a follower and catches up (log truncation may occur)

items.q: What are the key producer configurations for high throughput? ⭐

head: **Config**
**Default**
**Recommended for Throughput**
**Effect**
rows: Larger batches = fewer network round trips
Wait to fill batches; increases latency but boosts throughput
Reduces message size; LZ4 is fastest
More buffer for high- volume producers

items.q: What are the key consumer configurations for high throughput?

head: **Config**
**Default**
**Tuning Tip**
rows: Increase to 1024+ to reduce fetches; waits for more data
Max wait for fetch.min.bytes to be met
Increase for batch processing; adjust with processing speed
Per-partition fetch size; increase for large messages
Set false for manual commit control

items.q: How does Kafka achieve such high throughput?

a.text: Kafka achieves high throughput through several design choices:

items: **Sequential disk I/O:** Kafka appends records sequentially to log files, which is much faster than random reads/writes
**Zero-copy transfer:** Uses sendfile() system call to transfer data from disk to network without copying to user space
**Batching:** Producers batch multiple records into a single network request
**Compression:** Batches can be compressed (gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd)
**Page cache:** Kafka relies on the OS page cache, avoiding double-buffering in JVM heap
**Partitioning:** Multiple partitions allow concurrent parallel reads/writes

modules.title: Kafka Streams & Kafka Connect
modules.summary: Kafka Streams vs consumer biasa, KStream vs KTable, state store, serta source/sink connector di Kafka Connect.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: What is Kafka Streams? How is it different from Kafka Consumer? ⭐

a.text: Kafka Streams is a client-side library for building real-time stream processing applications. Unlike a simple consumer, Kafka Streams provides:

items: **Stateful processing:** Maintains local state stores (RocksDB by default)
**Windowing:** Time-based and session-based windowed aggregations
**Exactly-once processing:** Built-in EOS support
**Join operations:** Stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table joins
**KStream / KTable abstraction:** KStream = unbounded event stream; KTable = changelog/snapshot

items.q: What is the difference between KStream and KTable?

head: **Aspect**
**KStream**
**KTable**
rows: Stateful — latest value per key stored

items.q: What is a State Store in Kafka Streams?

a.text: A State Store is a local storage mechanism used by Kafka Streams tasks to maintain stateful data (counts, aggregations, joins). Key characteristics:

items: **Default implementation:** RocksDB (persistent) or in-memory HashMap
**Changelog topic:** State changes are backed up to a Kafka topic for fault recovery
**Recovery:** On restart, state is restored from the changelog topic
**Interactive queries:** State stores can be queried externally via queryableStoreName

items.q: What is Kafka Connect? What are Source and Sink Connectors?

a.text: Kafka Connect is a framework for reliably streaming data between Kafka and external systems (databases, file systems, cloud services, etc.) without writing custom producers/consumers.

items: **Source Connector:** Reads data FROM an external system INTO Kafka (e.g., JDBC Source reads from a database and writes to Kafka)
**Sink Connector:** Reads data FROM Kafka and writes TO an external system (e.g., JDBC Sink writes Kafka messages to a database)
**Workers:** Kafka Connect workers are distributed, fault-tolerant, and scalable processes that run connectors
**Tasks:** Each connector is split into tasks; tasks run in parallel across workers

a.text: Common connectors:

items: Debezium (CDC from MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB)
JDBC Connector (relational databases)
S3 Sink Connector
Elasticsearch Sink Connector
HDFS Connector

modules.title: Kafka Lanjutan: Konsep, Security & Monitoring
modules.summary: Log compaction, KRaft vs ZooKeeper, delivery semantics, schema evolution, mekanisme keamanan, dan metrik yang wajib dimonitor.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: What is Log Compaction in Kafka?

a.text: Log compaction is a retention mechanism that retains only the LATEST record for each key, instead of retaining records for a fixed time or size. This is useful for:

items: Event sourcing and changelog topics
Database change-data-capture (CDC) snapshots
Topics used as KTables in Kafka Streams

a.text: How it works:

items: A background cleaner thread periodically scans dirty log segments
For each key, only the record with the highest offset is retained
A null value (tombstone) for a key marks it for eventual deletion

items.q: What is KRaft mode in Kafka? Why is ZooKeeper being removed? ⭐

a.text: KRaft (Kafka Raft Metadata mode) is the self-managed metadata quorum that replaces ZooKeeper in Kafka 3.x and later. Reasons for removal:

items: **Operational complexity:** ZooKeeper requires a separate cluster with separate monitoring and ops
**Scalability limits:** ZooKeeper becomes a bottleneck with very large numbers of partitions
**Startup time:** With ZooKeeper, controller failover can take 30+ seconds; KRaft makes it milliseconds
**Unified security model:** Single security config instead of managing two separate systems

a.text: KRaft uses a Raft-based consensus protocol within Kafka brokers themselves to manage cluster metadata. Kafka 3.3+ supports KRaft for production use.

items.q: Explain Kafka delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once.

head: **Semantics**
**Description**
**Configuration**
**Risk**
rows: Message delivered 0 or 1 times; may be lost
Message delivered 1+ times; may be duplicated
Message delivered exactly once; no loss, no duplication

items.q: How do you handle schema evolution in Kafka?

a.text: Schema evolution is managing changes to message formats over time. Approaches:

items: **Schema Registry (Confluent):** Centralizes Avro/JSON/Protobuf schemas; enforces compatibility rules; producers register schemas, consumers fetch them by ID
**Backward compatibility:** New schema can read data written by old schema (add optional fields with defaults)
**Forward compatibility:** Old schema can read data written by new schema (remove optional fields)
**Full compatibility:** Both backward and forward compatible

items.q: What security mechanisms does Kafka support?

items: **Authentication:** SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, SASL/GSSAPI (Kerberos), mTLS (mutual TLS)
**Encryption in transit:** TLS/SSL for all broker-client and broker-broker communication
**Authorization:** ACLs (Access Control Lists) using AclAuthorizer; can also use OPA or custom authorizers
**Encryption at rest:** Not natively supported; use filesystem/volume encryption

items.q: What are important Kafka metrics to monitor?

a.text: Broker Metrics

items: kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec — message ingestion rate
kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions — must be 0
kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=ActiveControllerCount — must be exactly 1
kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=IsrShrinksPerSec — ISR shrinks indicate issues

a.text: Consumer Metrics

items: records-lag-max — maximum consumer lag; critical for monitoring backlog
fetch-rate — number of fetch requests per second
bytes-consumed-rate — throughput consumed

a.text: Producer Metrics

items: record-send-rate — records sent per second
record-error-rate — failed sends; should be 0
request-latency-avg — average request latency to broker

a.text: **Note:** *Tools commonly used: Prometheus + Grafana with JMX Exporter, Confluent Control Center, Burrow (consumer lag monitoring), and LinkedIn's Cruise Control for rebalancing.*

modules.title: Kafka: Pola, Best Practice & Soal Skenario
modules.summary: Pola desain Kafka, kesalahan umum, dead letter queue, lalu soal skenario: sistem order, urutan pesan lintas partisi, zero data loss.
modules.source: Apache Kafka Interview Preparation Guide (Java Edition)

items.q: What are common Kafka design patterns?

items: **Event Sourcing:** All state changes are stored as a sequence of events in Kafka; current state derived by replaying events
**CQRS:** Command Query Responsibility Segregation — commands write to Kafka; queries read from materialized views (KTable)
**Saga Pattern:** Distributed transactions using choreography (events) or orchestration (commands) across microservices
**Outbox Pattern:** Write to local DB + outbox table atomically; a Kafka connector reads outbox and publishes events (avoids dual-write)
**Fan-out:** Multiple consumer groups independently read the same topic for different processing pipelines
**Dead Letter Queue (DLQ):** Failed messages are written to a separate DLQ topic for manual inspection/retry

items.q: What are common Kafka pitfalls and how to avoid them?

items: **Uncontrolled rebalancing:** Use static group membership (group.instance.id) and tune session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms
**Consumer lag buildup:** Monitor lag metrics; increase parallelism (more partitions + more consumers); optimize processing logic
**Duplicate processing:** Use idempotent consumers (check record ID before processing) or enable exactly-once semantics
**Large messages:** Kafka is optimized for small-medium messages (<1MB); store large payloads in S3/blob store and send reference in Kafka
**Hot partitions:** Poor key choice (e.g., all messages with same key) overloads one partition; use high-cardinality keys
**Not monitoring consumer lag:** Always monitor records-lag-max; set alerts when lag grows beyond threshold
**Incorrect offset management:** Committing offsets BEFORE processing causes data loss; process THEN commit

items.q: How do you implement a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) pattern in Kafka?

a.text: A DLQ pattern routes messages that fail processing to a separate topic for later inspection or reprocessing.

items.q: How would you design a Kafka-based order processing system? ⭐

a.text: High-level design:

items: **Topics:** orders (raw), orders-validated, orders-fulfilled, orders-dlq
**Partitioning:** Partition by order-id or customer-id for locality; use 12–24 partitions for scalability
**Producers:** Order service publishes to orders topic with acks=all, idempotence enabled
**Validation consumer:** Consumer group validates orders; writes to orders-validated or orders-dlq
**Fulfillment consumer:** Separate consumer group reads orders-validated; triggers warehouse/payment
**Monitoring:** Alert on orders-dlq lag and consumer lag on each stage
**Schema:** Avro schemas with Schema Registry for type safety and evolution

items.q: How would you handle message ordering in Kafka across partitions?

a.text: Kafka only guarantees order within a single partition. Strategies to handle ordering:

items: **Single partition (simplest):** Use one partition — total ordering guaranteed but zero parallelism
**Key-based routing:** Ensure all related messages (same order ID) go to the same partition by using the order ID as the message key
**Application-level sequencing:** Embed a sequence number in the message and reorder in the consumer
**Kafka Streams windowing:** Use time-based windows to collect and sort events before processing

a.text: **Note:** *For most systems, per-entity ordering (same customer or order) is sufficient. Use the entity ID as the Kafka message key to guarantee ordering for all events related to that entity.*

items.q: How would you ensure zero data loss in Kafka?

a.text: Configuration checklist for zero data loss:

items: **Producer:** acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, retries=MAX_INT, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
**Broker:** replication.factor>=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
**Consumer:** enable.auto.commit=false, process-then-commit pattern
**Topic:** retention.bytes and retention.ms configured adequately
**Monitoring:** Alert on under-replicated partitions and broker failures immediately

Broker, Topic, Partition, Offset, Producer, Consumer, Consumer Group, ZooKeeper/KRaft
Key-based (murmur2 hash) or round-robin; ordering guaranteed per partition only
Sequential ID per record within a partition; consumer tracks position
Serialize → Partition → Accumulate batch → Background Sender → Ack
0=no ack, 1=leader ack, all=all ISR ack (best durability)
Each partition assigned to ONE consumer in group; multiple groups = broadcast
Triggered by join/leave/timeout; stop-the-world; use CooperativeStickyAssignor
Leader handles R/W; followers copy; ISR = in-sync replicas
Min ISR that must ack (with acks=all); use RF=3, minISR=2 in prod
Client library for stateful stream processing; KStream vs KTable
Replaces ZooKeeper with Raft-based metadata within Kafka itself (Kafka 3.3+)
Multiple topics per stage, partition by entity key, monitor lag & DLQ
